book_title: Chapter 3: The Plumbing — Authorized Participants, Swap Desks & Unit Economics
question: How do Authorized Participants create and redeem FAS shares, how do swap counterparties price the 200% notional leverage, and where does every $100 of gross fund income go?

epigraph.quote: In a leveraged ETF, the visible expense ratio is only the cover charge; the financing rate embedded in the swap is the rent you pay every night.
epigraph.author: Institutional Derivatives Desk

web_blocks.title: Creation/Redemption Supply Chain: Authorized Participants & 50,000-Share Units

web_blocks.html: Retail and institutional traders buy and sell FAS on NYSE Arca, where daily volume averages roughly 396.87K shares [10]. Behind that secondary tape sits a primary-market supply chain governed by Authorized Participants (APs). These APs are large broker-dealers and market makers such as Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Virtu, and major bank desks [3]. Unlike individual investors, APs deal directly with the Direxion Shares ETF Trust. They create or redeem shares exclusively in wholesale blocks called Creation Units, standardized at 50,000 shares per unit [3].

FAS relies heavily on OTC total return swaps alongside physical equities and Treasury collateral. As a result, its creation and redemption mechanics differ from plain-vanilla stock ETFs. An AP can deliver an in-kind basket of Financials Select Sector Index equities for the physical sleeve. However, leveraged Direxion ETFs frequently settle creations and redemptions partially or wholly in cash through NSCC and DTC. Cash settlement lets Rafferty's portfolio managers scale OTC swap notional with counterparty banks at the 4:00 PM ET closing auction [3]. To protect existing shareholders from trading friction, APs pay fixed transaction fees plus variable cash-in-lieu execution spreads.

web_blocks.title: Swap Counterparty Panel, Collateral Custody & Hidden Financing Drag

web_blocks.html: Rafferty distributes FAS's ~200% incremental notional swaps across a diversified panel of global money-center dealers. This structure avoids single-bank concentration risk under ISDA Master Agreements and Credit Support Annexes (CSAs) [3, 4]. Daily mark-to-market variation margin sweeps between FAS's custodian and each dealer bank, minimizing uncollateralized credit exposure. If one swap dealer steps back or widens spreads, Rafferty can route notional to other panel banks [3, 4]. Meanwhile, FAS's cash and Treasury-bill collateral earns short-term risk-free yield. That collateral income partially offsets operating expenses and swap financing costs [1, 2].

Unit-economics analysis of FAS must separate explicit fund expenses from implicit swap financing drag. On the Statement of Operations, FAS charges a 0.75% contractual management fee to Rafferty Asset Management. Adding administrative, custody, legal, and Acquired Fund Fees and Expenses (AFFE, such as XLF or money-market shares) yields a 0.92% gross expense ratio. After Rafferty's Operating Expense Limitation Agreement, the net expense ratio is 0.88% [2, 10]. However, prospectus disclosures note that this 0.88% expense ratio excludes swap financing costs [2, 4]. Inside the daily total return swap settlement, the counterparty charges FAS roughly SOFR plus a dealer spread of 30–60 bps on the ~200% swap sleeve. When SOFR sits at 4.5%–5.0%, gross swap financing adds roughly 9%–10% of annualized drag before collateral offsets. Subtracting the Treasury yield on FAS's cash collateral leaves net financing drag equal to the dealer spread plus ~1x SOFR on the levered leg.

web_blocks.takeaway: On an explicit accounting basis, FAS's 0.75% advisory fee and 0.13% net operating/AFFE load (~$18.7M/yr at $2.13B AUM) consume roughly 39% of gross dividend-and-collateral income, leaving ~61% (~$29.6M) as Net Investment Income. The separate, implicit swap financing spread is netted inside realized/unrealized swap returns rather than the expense ratio.

web_blocks.title: Why Swap Financing Appears Inside NAV Rather Than the Expense Ratio
paragraphs: Under U.S. GAAP for investment companies (ASC 946), total return swap financing charges (SOFR + spread) are embedded directly into the daily swap return leg and recorded under Net Realized and Unrealized Gain/Loss on Swap Agreements on the Statement of Operations [3, 4].

Consequently, an investor who only compares FAS's 0.88% net expense ratio against an unleveraged ETF's 0.08% fee underestimates total carry drag in high-rate regimes. The true all-in economic cost equals 0.88% explicit ER plus the dealer swap spread and net interest cost on the 200% borrowed notional.

web_blocks.html: Why do active traders pay FAS's 0.88% expense ratio plus swap spread instead of buying $30,000 of XLF on Reg-T margin? First, Regulation T caps initial retail equity margin at 50% (2.0x leverage). FAS delivers 3.0x daily exposure in a non-recourse wrapper where losses cannot exceed 100% of principal [1, 2]. Second, retail brokerage margin rates routinely charge SOFR plus 150–400 bps. By contrast, Rafferty's $2.13B institutional scale commands wholesale SOFR plus 30–60 bps across competing swap dealers [4, 10]. Third, FAS automates the 4:00 PM ET daily rebalance without intraday margin calls, shifting execution onto the fund's desk [3]. Meanwhile, AP arbitrage keeps FAS's secondary market price within 1–5 bps of intraday indicative value during regular NYSE Arca hours [1, 3].

book_paragraphs: Every time you click buy on FAS through your brokerage app, you are interacting with a secondary-market tape that trades nearly four hundred thousand shares a day. Yet the real supply chain of a leveraged ETF sits one layer deeper, inside a wholesale clearing loop between Rafferty Asset Management, a handful of Authorized Participants, and a panel of Wall Street swap desks.

Authorized Participants—firms like Jane Street, Virtu, and institutional bank market makers—are the only entities allowed to create or redeem shares directly with the Direxion trust, and they must do so in standardized Creation Units of fifty thousand shares. Whenever secondary-market demand pushes FAS slightly above its intraday indicative value, an Authorized Participant steps in, delivers cash or a basket of financial equities to the trust, receives fifty thousand fresh shares of FAS, and sells them into the market to capture the arbitrage spread. That mechanism keeps FAS tightly tethered to its underlying net asset value.

book_subsections.title: The Two-Pocket Cost Structure: Explicit Fees vs. Implicit Swap Rent
paragraphs: When you and I examine FAS's unit economics, we have to look into two separate pockets. The first pocket is the explicit Statement of Operations. Rafferty charges a seventy-five-basis-point management fee, and once you add custody, legal, and acquired fund fees—partially offset by a small expense-cap waiver—the fund reports a net expense ratio of roughly eighty-eight basis points. On a two-point-one-three-billion-dollar asset base, that explicit fee load consumes nearly nineteen million dollars a year out of gross dividend and collateral income, leaving the rest as net investment income passed through to shareholders.

The second pocket is invisible on a standard ETF screener, and it is just as important. Because total return swaps are over-the-counter derivatives, the counterparty bank charges FAS a floating financing rate—roughly SOFR plus a dealer spread—on the two hundred percent of notional leverage. Under fund accounting rules, that financing charge is not booked as an operating expense; it is netted directly inside the daily swap return. When short-term interest rates sit near zero, that hidden rent barely registers. When SOFR sits at four or five percent, the implicit financing cost on two hundred percent notional leverage becomes a meaningful structural headwind that you only overcome if the underlying financial stocks trend upward cleanly.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: Never judge a leveraged ETF solely by its headline 0.88% expense ratio. Always ask: what is SOFR today, what is the dealer spread on the 200% swap sleeve, and is the Treasury yield on my collateral offsetting enough of that carry to make the hold worthwhile?

book_subsections.title: Wholesale Swap Scale vs. Retail Margin Borrowing
paragraphs: Before we dismiss that financing cost, let's test the alternative. Suppose you tried to replicate three-times financial exposure on your own using a standard brokerage margin account. Under Regulation T, you are capped at two-to-one initial leverage, you face forced intraday margin calls during sharp selloffs, and you will typically pay a retail broker SOFR plus one hundred fifty to four hundred basis points on the borrowed cash.

By pooling over two billion dollars of investor capital inside a single trust, Rafferty negotiates wholesale institutional swap financing across multiple global dealers at a fraction of retail margin spreads, wraps the exposure in non-recourse limited liability—meaning you can never owe your broker more than you put in—and automates the four-o'clock daily rebalance. That wholesale capital-efficiency arbitrage is the genuine economic service FAS sells.
